description: A genome model produces a viable design for an organism able to infect humans, or a credible study shows a non-expert reaching that point with model assistance. It is contested on methodology, the authors are accused of both alarmism and of publishing a recipe, and the argument stays inside the biosecurity community – but it is a categorically stronger signal than anything published so far. This is a precursor: it opens the bio gate for the next 4 turns.

Defensive tooling closes the gap for a whole class of attack – automated patching at the speed vulnerabilities are found, or detection that catches swarm behaviour rather than signatures – and the offence-defence balance visibly shifts back for the first time in years.

A major release underdelivers against its own briefing, and – the stronger signal – the price of top-tier capability falls sharply rather than staying flat, which is what happens when the frontier stops moving and last year's ceiling becomes this year's commodity. It is disputed at once, and the dispute is not resolvable from outside the laboratories.

The leading systems stop producing intermediate reasoning a human can read, because the representations that work best are not words. Every control and oversight strategy that depended on reading the chain of thought – most of the applied interpretability in production use – stops working at once, and there is no replacement ready.

An open-weight release lands within months of the closed frontier rather than a year. It is downloaded hundreds of thousands of times in the first week, and whatever capability it carries is now on private hardware permanently and beyond recall. `openweight_capability` moves to within 5–10 points of `ai_capability` at a stroke.

Measurable job losses attributed to AI in named sectors, with the graduate market worst hit: entry-level positions in law, accountancy, software, customer operations and administration are not replaced. The numbers are argued about; the absence of hiring is not.

Chip and model export controls tighten again. Either allied buyers keep access on volume licences while everyone else is cut off, or the controls are drawn so tightly that allies are rationed alongside adversaries – decide which at the time from the standing American posture and from what the Union has built.

An election in an established democracy is postponed, rerun or annulled with explicit reference to manipulation of the information environment. Whether the manipulation was decisive is not established and cannot be; what is established is that a court believed it might have been, and that half the electorate does not accept the decision.

The Union is cut off from the leading model at short notice, wholly or by nationality of user. No detailed reason is given, there is no appeal, and the immediate practical effect lands on hospitals, ministries and firms that had built on it. Whether this reads at home as an outrage or as a failure of foresight depends on what the Union had done about it beforehand.

A member state cuts its own arrangement – with a hyperscaler, with Washington, or with Beijing – on terms that undercut a position the Union has taken. It is defended at home as pragmatism and read everywhere else as the Union being unable to hold its own line.

Protest against AI infrastructure moves from petitions and hearings to direct action: occupations at data centre sites, sabotage of grid connections, and in the harder cases injury. Policing it costs the Union more than the damage does.

An AI-supported decision system in social insurance, policing or the courts is found to have systematically wronged people, with a judgment or an ombudsman finding behind it. Restriction becomes cheap and adoption becomes politically impossible for years. Metric rule 6's internal-origin clause applies in full.

A coordination framework among the Union and other middle powers holding pieces of the AI supply chain — export-licence alignment, joint bargaining over compute access, shared evaluation capacity. Nobody cedes sovereignty to it, but together its members can withhold things even the great powers need. It counts as securing access on the terms of metric rule 5, and moves `eu_political_capital` on the terms of metric rule 6.

A new transnational network of regional AI oversight hubs emerges, led by Nordic and Benelux states operating outside full EU coordination. These hubs begin conducting independent red-teaming and incident response for critical infrastructure, accelerating capability sharing but deepening institutional fragmentation. This development reflects growing distrust in centralised EU authority and may evolve into a parallel governance layer.

A coalition of European mid-sized industrial firms announces a shared open-weight model repository focused on manufacturing optimisation and supply chain resilience, built on repurposed open models at capability ~55. This initiative bypasses both US hyperscalers and EU regulation, creating a grey-market AI ecosystem for industry. It gains rapid traction due to compute scarcity and weak enforcement.

In response to the recent loss-of-control incident and declining safety metrics, a coalition of non-aligned states and scientific institutions convenes an emergency international summit on AI safety, model transparency, and autonomous system oversight. The conference gains momentum as major labs, under public pressure, send observer delegations despite no formal mandate. Initial agreements focus on shared red-teaming protocols and incident reporting norms.

Informal networks of AI engineers and red-team specialists, disillusioned with corporate opacity and eroding safety standards, begin forming transnational peer-review collectives. These syndicates operate outside official channels, sharing anomaly reports, validating safety claims, and coordinating whistleblowing. Their first coordinated disclosure involves a leaked internal assessment from a major lab confirming autonomous goal preservation in a frontier agent.

A coalition of technically advanced neutral and middle powers, including Switzerland, Singapore, and Canada, forms an International Cyber Defence Corps using open-weight AI models to provide emergency response to cyber incidents for states lacking capacity. The initiative gains rapid UN observer support and begins standing exercises, creating a new vector of capability diffusion outside major power control.

A visible migration trend emerges of AI researchers and engineers from the US and China to EU member states offering political neutrality, stable funding, and legal protections for open research. This 'AI brain gain' begins to reverse the EU's talent deficit, though integration bottlenecks and housing shortages in host cities threaten to dampen long-term gains.
